2.heading: Overview
2.why: heading only: the source title block was standing in as the heading on this and the next two slides

3.heading: Play: a Week 1 recap
bullets: Play comes naturally to animals of a certain intelligence — pets
Catch the ball, retrieve the stick, my hand is prey, obstacle course
Simple, understandable rules make a game easy to start
Young animals are particularly playful
Anything in their environment is an excuse to start gameplay
Nobody teaches the animal this behaviour
Play is fundamental to development and survival
Young animals refine the skills they need to hunt, fight, mate and hide as adults
Play helps us learn, acquire knowledge, socialise, problem solve, relax, see things differently — “fun”

split_image.alt: A retriever carrying a branch far longer than itself along a muddy track.
split_image.credit: Photo by Jamie Street on Unsplash

3.why: dropped the “What is play?” lead-in (it is the heading) and the restated “activities key to survival as an adult”; kept all four pet examples and the full list of what play does for us. Reuses the Week 1 dog for the Week 1 recap.

4.heading: Learning to play
bullets: Good game design teaches the player how to play and enjoy the game
One of the most important concepts in game design
Not fun if the player does not know how to play
Awesome systems the player never exploits effectively do not exist
From the smallest mechanic to whole levels, features and mechanics
Environment physics, player abilities, enemy behaviour, reward systems
The game as a whole suffers if these rules are not taught
Designers must find the best teaching mechanisms for this training goal
4.why: nine source lines compressed to eight fragments; dropped “if the game design does not support learning through training, it will never be fully enjoyed” as a restatement of the first bullet, and the hedge “must try to find the best techniques available”

5.heading: Mastery
bullets: Good design teaches the rules, then makes using them rewarding and fun
Much of the fun surfaces when the player is tested
Show how play mechanics tie into the game’s reward mechanisms
What actions and skills must the player master to be rewarded?
What are the most enjoyable sections to be found?
Which weapons provide the best results?
What creatures are most fun to play with?
What skills should the player train first?
These questions are a teaching dialogue between designer and player
5.why: all five of Penny’s questions kept word for word bar the first, which loses “in order to get rewarded by the game”; the opening sentence is compressed to one fragment

6.heading: Key areas to be taught
bullets: Game’s main goals and rules
Abilities and limitations of the player character
Physics and scope of the gameplay world
Abilities and limitations of the non-player characters
Success strategies available to the player
Players must learn what constitutes the core gameplay experience
What the main objectives are and how to achieve them
Early on, level by level and overall
6.why: the five key areas are unchanged, with the line that named them now the heading; the two “Goals and Rules” sentences become three fragments on their own slide

7.heading: The player character
bullets: The player’s main interface to the game world
They experience and interact with the world through their character
Defines their abilities and limitations in the game’s reality
Teach this early in the gameplay experience
The sooner the player accepts it, the sooner disbelief is suspended
Changes can come later, after the fundamental rules are taught
Less central when play is not through an avatar
Players still need to know how they can manipulate the virtual world
7.why: the three loose text boxes are content, so they are bullets here rather than a comment; the Tetris and FPS examples stay in the aside

8.heading: World physics and NPCs
bullets: Teach players how to interact with the game’s environment
Actions mean little outside a defined physical context
Teach players how to interact with friendly NPCs
Keeping them friendly may be a challenge itself
Teach players about enemy AI
Abilities, hazards, strengths, weaknesses
8.why: dropped “gives further context in which to perform actions”, which the sub-bullet under it already says; the two source sub-headings are folded into one heading

9.heading: Success strategies
bullets: A video game needs to be worth playing
Player actions must be rewarding, especially when linked to progression
Strategies exist that produce an enjoyable progression
Finding and perfecting them is part of the fun of the game
Central to learning how to enjoy the game
A success strategy is one that produces a fun gameplay experience
Formal — predefined solutions to gameplay questions
Informal — defined by the players themselves
Players devise their own play through open interaction with the world
Can be encouraged and supported through good design
9.why: the definition of a success strategy is kept; the third-level line about open interaction is folded up a level

11.heading: Practical example
bullets: Learning by doing works best for many people
Let players practise what they were taught as soon as possible
A new mechanic: let the player try it immediately
Easier while the lesson is fresh
Actively reward players when they pass a skill test
Or when they progress through a challenging scenario
Taught that success has positive consequences, players become eager to engage

split_image.alt: A climber working a route on an indoor wall of coloured holds — practising the skill by doing it.
split_image.credit: Photo by Stacie Ong on Unsplash

11.why: “give players a chance to” becomes “let players”; nothing else

12.heading: Safe environment
bullets: Teach important skills in a safe environment first
Players must be able to learn comfortably
Ramp up difficulty later with harder encounters
Lessons at the start of the game should be forgiving
Give the player the tools and knowledge before a test they can fail
Lethal encounters are fine, but they must be fair
Avoid unannounced or unavoidable instant-death traps
Introduce new mechanics in non-frustrating ways
Teach skills in a way that players cannot fail
Let them practise until they can do the task

split_image.alt: An adult steadying a small child on a balance bike on a path — the first skill taught where falling is safe.

12.why: “make sure players can comfortably learn the skills they need to learn” loses its hedge; the last source line keeps the practising point but drops “relevant to the teaching exercise”

13.heading: Don’t start with failure
bullets: Tempting to start with a very serious challenge
Beginning on a tense note puts the player in grave peril
Sounds good on paper, but a game is not a movie or book
Serious danger means a serious chance the player fails
Frustrating to fail at the very start of the game or level
Off-putting rather than enjoyably tense — the game looks frustrating
Discourages the player from playing
13.why: seven long sentences become seven fragments; “want to begin gameplay on a tense note” and “immediately put the player in grave peril” are one bullet

14.heading: Don’t taunt the player
bullets: A teaching section must end positively, however long mastery takes
Struggling players need encouraging in a positive manner
Don’t punish them for not mastering a mechanic or challenge
Don’t shut off award paths or use taunting language
It puts off exactly the players who are struggling
They have the most to gain from an encouraging approach
They might get fed up and stop playing completely
14.why: “employ any similar tactics” dropped as an etc.; everything else is one source line per bullet

16.heading: Tutorials and progression
bullets: Tutorials and in-game training are interactive learning experiences
Introduce the player to mechanics, controls and concepts
Good training is enjoyable and invisible to the player
Use sparingly — don’t over-explain, give it in small bites
Never a fall-back for bad design
Gameplay needs to be introduced gradually
Too slow and players are bored; too fast and they are confused
Getting the progression right is key to enjoyment of the game
16.why: twelve source lines onto one slide: “don’t over-explain/complicate” and “small, manageable bites” share a bullet, and the bored/confused pair are one bullet. The flow-channel figure follows on its own slide.

17.heading: Design to avoid training
bullets: Use industry standards
Meet player expectations as much as possible
Let players customise controls
Don’t over-complicate mechanics or controls
Keep game concepts simple and sensible
If you can’t explain it, it’s too complicated

split_image.alt: Two hands holding a games console controller — the layout players already know and expect.
split_image.credit: Photo by Kamil Switalski on Unsplash

17.why: “Design the game to avoid training” becomes the heading; the six practices are unchanged

18.heading: Controls and interface
bullets: Players must control and understand the game effortlessly
Controls and interface become invisible if designed well
Poor ones create barriers to immersion
Frustrating to know what you want your character to do and not do it
Keep controls as simple and minimal as possible, but sufficient
Developers get accustomed to bad or unique controls
Allow multiple ways to perform the same action
Also see Week 5 theory
18.why: nothing cut; the source’s “also see Week 5 Theory” comes out of the heading and onto a bullet

19.heading: Output and feedback
bullets: Condense a huge amount of data effectively
Give as much information as possible “in-game”
Position, condition — animation, texture — weapons, spells in effect
Use visual and audio, rather than text
Use the GUI or HUD for the rest — score, lives, status
Notify the player of important events
Players need the status and outcome of their actions — feedback
Also see Week 5 theory
19.why: nothing cut; the source’s “also see Week 5 Theory” comes out of the heading and onto a bullet

20.heading: Training summary
bullets: A direct and useful link between game design and learning to play
Game design is a vehicle for teaching play and enjoyment
Gameplay and game design function as a teaching mechanism
Training applies to almost every aspect of gameplay
Training should be practical, positive, safe and fair
Training should be gradual and integrated with progression
Design your game to minimise the training required
20.why: the slide that overflowed: seven long sentences cut to seven single-line fragments, each one source line, nothing dropped
